lessons.title: Variables & Types
lessons.content:
# Variables & Types

Go is a statically typed, compiled language with a focus on simplicity.

### Declarations
- `var x int = 10`
- `x := 10` (Short declaration, only inside functions)

### Basic Types
- `bool`, `string`
- `int`, `int8`, `int16`, `int32`, `int64`
- `uint`, `uintptr`
- `byte` (alias for `uint8`)
- `rune` (alias for `int32`, represents a Unicode code point)
- `float32`, `float64`
- `complex64`, `complex128`

### Zero Values
Variables declared without an explicit initial value are given their zero value (`0` for numbers, `false` for booleans, `""` for strings).

lessons.title: Control Flow
lessons.content:
# Control Flow

### If/Else
```go
if x > 0 {
    return "positive"
} else {
    return "negative"
}
```
You can also have an init statement before the condition: `if v := math.Pow(x, n); v < lim { ... }`.

### For Loops
Go only has one looping construct: `for`.
```go
for i := 0; i < 10; i++ {
    sum += i
}
```
It can also act as a `while` loop: `for sum < 1000 { ... }`.

### Switch
```go
switch os := runtime.GOOS; os {
case "darwin":
    fmt.Println("OS X.")
default:
    fmt.Printf("%s.\n", os)
}
```

lessons.title: Functions
Structs & Pointers
lessons.content:
# Structs & Pointers

### Structs
A collection of fields.
```go
type Vertex struct {
    X int
    Y int
}
```

### Pointers
Go has pointers. A pointer holds the memory address of a value. There is no pointer arithmetic.
```go
i := 42
p := &i
fmt.Println(*p) // read i through the pointer p
*p = 21         // set i through the pointer p
```

lessons.title: Methods
Interfaces
lessons.content:
# Interfaces

An interface type is defined as a set of method signatures.

```go
type Abser interface {
    Abs() float64
}
```

In Go, interfaces are implemented implicitly. A type implements an interface by implementing its methods. There is no explicit declaration of intent, no "implements" keyword.

lessons.title: Goroutines
lessons.content:
# Goroutines

A goroutine is a lightweight thread managed by the Go runtime.

```go
go f(x, y, z)
```
starts a new goroutine running `f(x, y, z)`. The evaluation of `f`, `x`, `y`, and `z` happens in the current goroutine and the execution of `f` happens in the new goroutine.

lessons.title: Channels
lessons.content:
# Channels

Channels are a typed conduit through which you can send and receive values with the channel operator, `<-`.

```go
ch := make(chan int)
ch <- v    // Send v to channel ch.
v := <-ch  // Receive from ch, and assign value to v.
```
By default, sends and receives block until the other side is ready. This allows goroutines to synchronize without explicit locks or condition variables.

lessons.title: Select
lessons.content:
# Select

The `select` statement lets a goroutine wait on multiple communication operations.

```go
select {
case c <- x:
    x, y = y, x+y
case <-quit:
    fmt.Println("quit")
    return
}
```
A `select` blocks until one of its cases can run, then it executes that case. It chooses one at random if multiple are ready.
